claims.claim: A right is standardly analyzed as an entitlement or claim that generates duties in others: a claim-right of A that B do φ means B has a duty to A to do φ.

Moral rights are grounded in moral reasons, whereas legal rights derive from the laws of a society; a right can be morally justified without being legally recognized, and legally recognized without being morally justified.

A negative right entitles its holder to non-interference, while a positive right entitles its holder to provision of some good or service; the right against assault is a classic negative right and a right to welfare assistance a prototypical positive right.

The negative/positive distinction is popular among some normative theorists, especially those with a libertarian leaning, but its boundary is debated: enforcing any right costs resources, and some rights are neither simply negative nor simply positive.

Wesley Hohfeld (1879-1918) distinguished four basic legal incidents - the privilege (or liberty), the claim, the power, and the immunity - each with a distinctive logical form; a privilege is the absence of a duty not to act, a claim correlates with a duty owed to the holder, a power is the ability to alter one's own or another's incidents, and an immunity protects against another's power.
Correlativity: if A has a claim that B φ, then B has a duty to A to φ; every claim-right correlates with a duty in at least one duty-bearer.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 (General Assembly resolution 217 A) as a common standard of achievements for all peoples and all nations.

The UDHR was a response to the experience of the Second World War; its drafting proceeded through the UN Commission on Human Rights - chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt and composed of eighteen members - and a formal drafting committee drawn from eight states, after the General Assembly took up the matter at its first session in 1946.

The UDHR sets out thirty articles (Article 1 opens: all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights), has been translated into more than 500 languages, and is widely recognized as having inspired more than seventy human-rights treaties.

The philosophical foundations of human rights are contested: some justify rights by the status or nature of persons (deontological approaches), others by the valuable states of affairs rights bring about (instrumental, consequentialist approaches), and moral relativists deny that universally valid moral truths exist at all.

Whether rights are universal, whether groups (as well as individuals) can hold rights, and whether rights can genuinely conflict are open philosophical debates; the extent to which rights are compatible with non-individualistic frameworks remains unsettled.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether negative and positive rights form a clean distinction with different costs of satisfaction.
positions: Some theorists (often libertarian-leaning) hold that negative rights entitle holders to non-interference and are easier to satisfy, since they only require forbearance.
Other theorists note that enforcing any right costs resources and that many rights mix elements, so the boundary is not fixed.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the negative/positive distinction as widely used but explicitly notes that its boundary is debated, without endorsing either camp.

positions: Status-based (deontological) theories: persons have attributes that make it fitting to ascribe rights to them.
Instrumental (consequentialist) theories: respect for rights brings about valuable states of affairs.
Moral relativism: there are no universally valid moral truths, so human rights are products of particular societies and histories.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes each position neutrally and does not adjudicate among them.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether groups, as distinct from individuals, can hold rights.
positions: The interest theory can extend right-holding to entities with interests, including groups and institutions.
Other accounts, such as classic versions of the will theory, restrict rights to beings able to exercise control over duties.
Communitarian views vary from tempering individual-rights talk to defending group-level values.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the question as open and notes that different theories yield different answers.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether rights can genuinely conflict and how apparent conflicts should be handled.
positions: Rights often appear to conflict (e.g., a public right to protest versus a government's right to keep order), and some rights have priority in some circumstances but not others.
Specificationists argue that apparent conflicts dissolve once each right is stated with its qualifications.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson notes both positions and does not settle which is correct.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether human rights are universal or culturally relative.
positions: Universalists hold that all persons have the same basic rights regardless of society or history.
Relativists treat moral beliefs, including rights, as socially and historically contingent.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the debate neutrally, as the task requires.
